Umbrella people

Inuit

Inuit are living Indigenous peoples across the Arctic, with distinct regional names, communities and institutions. This broad guide uses Canadian Inuit accounts of Inuit Nunangat alongside a linguist’s explanation of regional naming. Iñupiat in Alaska and Kalaallit in Greenland have their own regional contexts; the sources here do not describe a single government or uniform set of beliefs.

Read the sources [3] Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks [4] Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Identity and homelands

Inuit communities extend across the Arctic. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami provides an Inuit-led introduction focused specifically on Inuit Nunangat in Canada.

Read the sources [1] Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami

02

Historical context

ITK’s Our 5000 Year Heritage connects Arctic history, environmental knowledge, colonial disruption, land claims, and self-government.

Read the sources [1] Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami [2] Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami

03

Living communities and further study

Regional identities and governments require separate study. Canadian national organizations do not speak for every Inuit community in Alaska or Greenland.

Read the sources [2] Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami

04

Names and scopes across Arctic regions

Lawrence Kaplan’s language-centre guide explains why specific regional names matter. It discusses Iñupiat in Alaska and Kalaallit in Greenland, and notes that Inuit can also have a wider organizational use including Yupik peoples. Such usage does not make regional identities interchangeable or establish anyone’s citizenship. Follow each community’s own naming context rather than using a broad label as a membership rule.

Read the sources [3] Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

05

Land, water and ice in Inuit Nunangat

ITK uses Inuit Nunangat for the connected land, waters and ice of the Canadian Inuit homeland. Its account distinguishes the Inuvialuit Settlement Region, Nunavut, Nunavik and Nunatsiavut. These are regional contexts for learning about communities and institutions; details from one region should not be applied across Alaska, Canada and Greenland.

Read the sources [4] Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami

06

Living communities, work and cultural continuity

ITK’s public account stresses sharing, respect for Elders and cooperation alongside work in music, arts, public service and other professions. That framing makes continuing community life visible rather than confining Inuit culture to an earlier era. The page mixes older population figures and forecasts, which are not used here; its institutional account is not a survey of every person’s beliefs or present circumstances.

Read the sources [4] Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami

07

History told in the present

In its historical introduction, ITK argues that Inuit should take a leading role in interpreting their own past. It presents oral transmission alongside archaeological and written evidence as ways of learning, connecting history with young people and future cultural life. This is the organization’s interpretive framing. The selected pages do not authorize access to restricted knowledge, validate every archaeological date in the booklet or replace locally authored histories.

Read the sources [2] Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami

08

A Nunavut institution’s public values framework

Nunavut’s Department of Culture and Heritage presents a framework that emphasizes caring relationships, learning through observation and repeated practice, cooperation, deliberation in decisions, and responsibility toward land and animals. It also describes a project intended to give Elders a stronger role in addressing community concerns. These are the department’s published priorities and stated purposes; the undated page does not establish measured results or present service availability. This institutional account belongs in its Nunavut context and should not be treated as a single creed for all Inuit communities.

Read the sources [5] Government of Nunavut, Department of Culture and Heritage

09

A public account of art and change in Kinngait

Writing in 2019, Nakasuk Alariaq describes Kiakshuk’s drawings, prints and carvings as recording a time of rapid change experienced by Inuit in the early twentieth century. The article also places Kiakshuk and Lukta Qiatsuk in late-1950s arts-programme work with James Houston that developed into the West Baffin Eskimo Co-operative. This is one writer’s account of a specific Kinngait art setting. The underlying artworks, interviews and co-operative records were not inspected for this guide.

Read the sources [6] Inuit Art Quarterly / Inuit Art Foundation
